seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-September, once the approach gully and talus are snow-free and the bolted pitches are dry

June.reason: Spring snow still fills the talus traverse and sits low on the route, and the vegetated gully to the notch is wet and slick.

July.reason: Snow clears from the talus and the cedar-and-heather gully through the month; early July can still have snow patches low on the route.

August.reason: Dry rock and a snow-free approach; start early, as the 4th-class gully to the notch is slow and parties above can knock loose blocks down.

September.reason: Still dry and cooler for the seven bolted pitches; shorter days and the first autumn snow usually arrive late in the month.

October.reason: Early snow and wet heather make the steep vegetated gully and the exposed north-face traverse on pitch 7 hazardous.

June.reason: Deep snow on the Terror Basin approach and a steep snow step below the 6,200 ft notch; the glacier and ridge are still loaded.

July.reason: The approach melts out through the month; early July may still need steep snow off the notch and consolidated glacier travel.

August.reason: Snow-free approach and dry rock on the six ridge pitches; the Terror Glacier crossing grows harder as crevasses open late in the month.

September.reason: Dry, stable weather is common, but the Terror Glacier is more broken and icy and shorter days tighten a long six-pitch day.

October.reason: First snows and short days make the brutal approach and a remote ridge with slow rescue a poor bet; permit office has closed for winter.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once the Aasgard gully is snow-free and the crack pitches have dried out

June.reason: Wet snow lingers on the Aasgard climbers' trail and descent slopes, and snowmelt seeps down the corner and crack pitches.

July.reason: The approach gully melts out through the month; early July can still hold wet snow on the talus and seepage on the harder pitches.

August.reason: Dry rock and long days; the west face stays shaded and cool until midday, a relief in peak heat. Wildfire smoke can foul some days.

September.reason: Often the driest, quietest month; the shaded west face gets cold, so start later and plan around shrinking daylight for a long day.

October.reason: The face stays cold in morning shade, days are short and early snow can return to the descent slopes; still feasible in a dry spell.

May.reason: Full snow cover, but north-side forest roads are usually still snowbound, adding miles, and the climbing pass season has just begun.

June.reason: Snow reaches 50 degrees with the rock pinch still filled in; roads melt out through the month, though the Killen Creek spur can lag.

July.reason: Roads are open and snow still covers the face early in the month; the crux pinch gets icier and sun cups deepen as July goes on.

August.reason: Snow thins to hard ice at the rock pinch and loose volcanic rock melts out, bringing rockfall; expect to need screws and two tools.

September.reason: Bare ice and exposed loose rock through the pinch; the climbing pass season ends at the end of the month.

September.reason: A dry-rock scramble on the southeast ridge, but a broken couloir, open crevasses and thick brush make the approach slow.

October.reason: New snow over bare glacier and loose rock, and early storms reload the couloir with slab.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to mid-August, once the approach and saddle gully melt out but before the Silver Glacier's schrunds and crevasses open wide

May.reason: The Ross Lake water taxi is not yet running, and deep snow still buries the Depot Creek and Silver Creek approaches and the saddle gully.

June.reason: The water taxi starts in mid-June, but slide alder above Silver Creek is still under wet snow and the saddle gully holds steep, avalanche-prone snow.

July.reason: Snow bridges still cover most crevasses and the two schrunds on the upper lobe, and the Silver Lake and Ouzel Lake camps have melted out.

August.reason: Stable weather and a snow-free approach; by late August the crevasses near 8,300 ft open and the upper-lobe schrunds get harder to cross.

September.reason: The thinning glacier is often bare ice with open crevasses and gaping schrunds, and the loose Class 4 summit step can glaze after early storms.

October.reason: The water taxi runs only until month's end, and the first autumn snow covers crevasses and ices the lichen-covered summit block.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to mid-September, when First Divide and the cross-country slopes above it are snow-free and days are still long

June.reason: Heavy Olympic snowpack still covers the upper North Fork Skokomish trail and First Divide, and the off-trail slopes to the summit are steep snow.

July.reason: The trail over First Divide usually melts out by mid-July, though snow patches linger on the cross-country line and north-facing slopes.

August.reason: The basin and the off-trail slopes above First Divide are dry, the streams are low, and the long days suit the 25-plus-mile round trip.

September.reason: Snow-free, bug-free travel through the meadows; the first fall storms usually hold off until late in the month.

October.reason: Autumn rain and early snow return to the Olympics, the unmarked route-finding gets harder in cloud, and short days stretch the long approach.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once the shaded Gendarme cracks and the traverse below it dry out and the approach is snow-free

June.reason: The Stuart Glacier couloir approach is easy on snow, but the north-facing Gendarme pitches and the gully traverse below them are often wet or icy.

July.reason: Snow and wet rock on the traverse below the Gendarme clear through the month, and the Sherpa Glacier still offers an easy snow descent.

August.reason: The offwidth and lieback are usually dry and the ridge is warm enough to jam; the Sherpa descent melts out, so parties use the Northwest Buttress instead.

September.reason: The rock stays dry but the shaded Gendarme is cold, the Stuart Glacier couloir approach turns to bare ice and rockfall, and days shorten.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas coat the north-facing cracks, and the short days leave little margin on an 11-pitch ridge before the Gendarme.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July and September, when the steep Kamikaze rock steps are dry and snow-free and the south-facing slope is not at peak heat

April.reason: Snow and ice linger near the Kamikaze ridge crest and on the rock steps, and the steep boot track is wet and slick with snowmelt.

May.reason: The lower boot track melts out, but patchy snow near the crest and wet, mossy rock steps make the Class 2-3 moves much harder than on the standard trail.

June.reason: The ridge crest is usually clear of snow by mid-June, though spring rain can still leave the mossy rock and roots slick.

July.reason: Dry, grippy rock steps and firm tread on the steep boot track, with long days that suit the Kamikaze-up, standard-trail-down loop.

August.reason: The rock is dry, but the southwest-facing slope bakes in afternoon heat, the tread turns loose and dusty, and there is no water above the falls.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures on the exposed slope and dry rock steps before the autumn rains return.

October.reason: Autumn rain wets the moss and roots again, and the seasonal trailhead gate closes earlier as the days shorten.

November.reason: Rain-soaked rock and the first snow near the crest make the steep boot track treacherous, especially on descent.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to September, when the ridge crest, the flat below Green Mountain and the summit scramble are all snow-free

March.reason: The trailhead is open, but the upper switchbacks, Rachor Pass and the summit rocks hold steep, icy snow that needs traction and an axe.

April.reason: The old logging-road grade melts out, but snow persists above about 3,500 ft and on the ridge crest, turning the upper trail into a snow slog.

May.reason: Lingering snow on the ridge crest and the flat below Green Mountain creates steep, icy sections on an otherwise Class 1-2 trail.

June.reason: The last snow near the ridge crest usually melts out during the month, leaving only short patches below the summit scramble.

July.reason: The whole trail and the brief Class 2 summit finish are snow-free, with long days well inside the trailhead gate hours.

August.reason: Dry trail and summit rocks; carry all your water, since there is none above Teneriffe Falls on the hot upper switchbacks.

September.reason: Snow-free and cooler than midsummer, with clear views from the summit before the autumn rains set in.

October.reason: Still usually snow-free, but the rain returns and the seasonal gate closes earlier as the days shorten.

November.reason: The first snow returns to the summit and ridge crest, and the short days leave little time before the trailhead gate closes.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August, after snow and ice clear the north buttress and before the Mustard Glacier approach turns to bare ice

June.reason: Snow and ice still plaster the north-facing buttress, and melting snow in the gullies and cols drives rockfall onto the route.

July.reason: By mid-July the buttress has usually cleared, and snow still covers the Mustard Glacier and the col crossing from Terror Camp.

August.reason: The rock is at its driest and the weather most stable, though the approach snowfields firm up and need crampons in the morning.

September.reason: The rock stays dry, but the Mustard Glacier and approach snowfields turn icy, the north face is cold, and shorter days tighten a long Grade IV.

October.reason: New snow and verglas coat the north face and the Crescent Creek approach, and the Marblemount permit office cuts its hours in mid-October.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, when snow still fills the loose notch gully but Crescent Creek Basin and the climber's track have melted out

May.reason: Deep snow covers the steep Terror Creek climber's track and Crescent Creek Basin, and the gully to the notch is an avalanche path.

June.reason: Snow fills the choss gully and smooths the approach, but the basin can be fully snow-covered and the gully slopes stay avalanche-prone.

July.reason: Firm snow still covers much of the loose gully while the basin opens up, though undercut snow and a moat may force moves along the edge.

August.reason: The gully melts out to loose rock and the chockstone near the notch, raising rockfall risk and requiring the low-5th crack moves.

September.reason: The fully snow-free gully is a loose rubble chute, cold nights ice the notch crack, and shorter days lengthen a long day from camp.

October.reason: Early snow over loose rock in the gully and on the ridge, and the Marblemount permit office cuts its hours in mid-October.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: February and March, when a deep, consolidated snowpack fills the drainages and the hidden gully and days are getting longer

December.reason: The snowpack is often thin or unconsolidated, leaving brush and choss exposed, and the road below Jefferson Pass may be blocked miles short.

January.reason: Snow usually covers the bushwhack drainages, but short days and storm-loaded slopes make the long approach from a snowed-in road risky.

February.reason: A deep, settled snowpack fills the drainages and the hidden gully; the classic mid-February weekend is a favourite window for this climb.

March.reason: Longer days and a consolidating snowpack give firm snow in the gully, though warm spells bring wet-slide cycles on the steep slopes.

April.reason: The road clears farther up, but spring warming loosens the chossy rock on the crux pitch and makes afternoon snow slopes wet and unstable.

May.reason: Snow is melting out of the lower drainages and the gully, exposing brush and loose rock and ending the snow-climb character of the route.

October.reason: Snow and ice can dust the wall and approach, and early storms precede the highway's winter closure through Washington Pass.

September.reason: Crevasses on the Mary Green descent are fully open, water on the crest is scarce, and shorter days squeeze a committing two-day line.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August, once the gully to the Concord-Lexington col is melted out and the north-facing rock is dry

September.reason: Still dry and quieter, but the shaded north face is cold, and an early storm leaves snow in the crack.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August, when the approach gullies are snow-free and the west rib is dry
